question.text: In the early years of a closed-ended Category I/II AIF, why is the fund NAV particularly difficult to rely on, per the J-curve discussion?

answer.text: Because management fees compound faster than portfolio growth
Because Indian GAAP prohibits fair-value accounting in early AIF years
Because SEBI requires NAV to be reported at cost in Year 1
Because unrealised investments form a large proportion of total fund value and underlying NAVs may not be representative of eventual cash-flow outcomes

explanation.text: The Logic: In the early years of a fund, underlying investments have not yet grown or been realised, so the unrealised component dominates total fund value. Underlying NAVs in this phase may not be representative of eventual cash-flow outcomes. As realisations occur over the fund's life, NAV converges toward the ultimate gross realisations — the NAV dimension of the classic J-curve. The Trap: Option A is a fee-drag story, which is a separate issue from NAV reliability. Option B is factually wrong — fair-value accounting under IND-AS 113 applies. Option C invents a non-existent SEBI cost-reporting rule. Note: The J-curve highlights that early-stage NAV is an estimate of unrealised value; realised proceeds (DPI) only build up as exits begin to occur.
